chapter.title: Foundations: measuring cost
chapter.summary: What an algorithm is, how to count its cost with Big-O, and how to read time and space off real code.

lessons.title: Algorithms and Big-O notation
lessons.summary: How to compare two solutions without running them, by asking how the work grows as the input grows.

parts.label: Concept
parts.body:
## What is an algorithm?

An **algorithm** is a precise, finite list of steps that turns an input into an output. A recipe is an algorithm. So is "find the largest number in a list": look at each number, remember the biggest so far, return it.

For most problems there are many correct algorithms. The interesting question is not *does it work?* but **how well does it keep working as the input gets big?**

## Why we don't just time it

Timing a program depends on your laptop, the language, and what else is running. Two people get different numbers for the same code. We want a measure that is about the **algorithm itself**.

The trick: count how the number of basic steps **grows as the input size `n` grows**. Not the exact count, just the shape of the growth.

## A worked example

Suppose you must check whether a list of `n` numbers contains a duplicate.

**Approach A: compare every pair.** For each number, compare it to every other number. That is about `n × n` comparisons.

**Approach B: remember what you have seen.** Walk the list once, keep a set of numbers seen so far, stop if the current one is already in the set. That is about `n` steps.

| n | Approach A (n²) | Approach B (n) |
|---|---|---|
| 10 | 100 | 10 |
| 1,000 | 1,000,000 | 1,000 |
| 1,000,000 | 1,000,000,000,000 | 1,000,000 |

At a million items, A is a million times more work. No faster laptop fixes that. This is why shape matters more than speed.

## Big-O in one sentence

**Big-O describes an upper bound on how an algorithm's cost grows with input size, ignoring constants and smaller terms.**

Three simplification rules:

1. **Drop constants.** `3n` and `100n` are both `O(n)`. They grow in the same straight line.
2. **Drop smaller terms.** `n² + 5n + 20` is `O(n²)`. At large `n`, the `n²` term swamps the rest.
3. **Different inputs, different letters.** Looping over list `a` then list `b` is `O(a + b)`, not `O(n)`. Nested loops over both are `O(a × b)`.

## The growth classes you must know

From fastest to slowest:

- **O(1) constant**: same work regardless of size. Reading `arr[5]`.
- **O(log n) logarithmic**: halve the problem each step. Binary search. Doubling the input adds *one* step.
- **O(n) linear**: touch every item once. Finding the max.
- **O(n log n) linearithmic**: the best general sorting algorithms.
- **O(n²) quadratic**: all pairs. Nested loops. Bubble sort.
- **O(2ⁿ) exponential**: all subsets. Naive recursive Fibonacci. Unusable past n ≈ 40.
- **O(n!) factorial**: all orderings. Brute-force travelling salesman.

A useful rule of thumb for interviews: with a time limit of about a second, you can do roughly **10⁸ simple operations**. So `n = 10⁵` allows `O(n log n)`, `n = 10⁴` allows `O(n²)`, and `n = 20` allows `O(2ⁿ)`.

## Best, average and worst case

Searching an unsorted list for a value: if it is the first item you are done in 1 step (**best case**). If it is last or absent you need `n` steps (**worst case**). Big-O usually quotes the **worst case**, because it is a guarantee. Quicksort is the famous example where average (`n log n`) and worst (`n²`) differ.

## Big-O, Big-Omega, Big-Theta

- **O(f)**: grows *no faster* than f (upper bound).
- **Ω(f)**: grows *at least as fast* as f (lower bound).
- **Θ(f)**: both. A tight bound.

In interviews people say "Big-O" when they mean the tight bound. Say `Θ` only if asked to be precise.

## Common mistakes

- Saying a loop is always `O(n)`. A loop that doubles `i` each time is `O(log n)`.
- Forgetting hidden costs: `string +=` in a loop copies the string each time and can make an `O(n)` loop secretly `O(n²)`.
- Treating `O(n)` and `O(2n)` as different. They are the same class.

keyPoints: Big-O measures how cost grows with input size, not how many seconds it takes.
Drop constants and smaller terms: 3n² + 5n + 2 is O(n²).
Different inputs get different letters: looping over a then b is O(a + b).
Big-O usually quotes the worst case; best and average cases can differ.
About 10⁸ simple operations fit in a second, so input size tells you the target complexity.

check.why: Drop constants (the 4) and smaller terms (100n and 7). Only n² dominates at large n.

check.q: A loop runs `for (i = 1; i < n; i *= 2)`. How many iterations?
check.why: i doubles each time, so it reaches n after about log₂ n steps.

lessons.title: Time and space complexity of real code
lessons.summary: A repeatable method for reading the complexity off loops, recursion and library calls, including space.

parts.label: Concept
parts.body:
## A four-step method

When an interviewer says "what is the complexity?", do this:

1. **Name the input size(s)**: `n` = length of the array, `m` = length of the second one, `V`/`E` for graphs.
2. **Count the work per loop level.** One loop over n: `n`. A loop inside it: multiply.
3. **Add sequential blocks, multiply nested ones.**
4. **Drop constants and smaller terms.**

## Pattern catalogue

**Single loop → O(n)**

```js
for (const x of arr) total += x;      // n
```

**Nested loop, both over n → O(n²)**

```js
for (i...n) for (j...n) work();       // n * n
```

**Nested with a shrinking inner range is still O(n²)**

```js
for (i = 0; i < n; i++)
  for (j = i + 1; j < n; j++) work(); // n + (n-1) + ... + 1 = n(n+1)/2
```

The sum `1 + 2 + ... + n` equals `n(n+1)/2`, which is `O(n²)`.

**Halving → O(log n)**

```js
while (lo <= hi) { mid = (lo + hi) >> 1; /* discard half */ }
```

**Loop with a log inside → O(n log n)**: for example, `n` binary searches, or sort then scan.

**Two pointers / sliding window → O(n)** even with a `while` inside a `for`, because each pointer only moves forward, so the total moves are at most `2n`.

## Recursion

Draw the **recursion tree**: how many calls, and how much work per call?

- `f(n) = f(n-1) + O(1)` (one call, shrink by 1): **O(n)** calls. Example: factorial.
- `f(n) = 2 f(n-1) + O(1)` (two calls, shrink by 1): **O(2ⁿ)**. Naive Fibonacci.
- `f(n) = 2 f(n/2) + O(n)` (two halves, linear merge): **O(n log n)**. Merge sort. The tree has `log n` levels and each level does `n` work in total.
- `f(n) = f(n/2) + O(1)`: **O(log n)**. Binary search.

## Space complexity

Space counts the **extra memory** your algorithm needs beyond the input:

- A few variables: **O(1)**.
- A new array or hash map of size n: **O(n)**.
- **Recursion uses the call stack**: depth `d` costs `O(d)` space. Recursing n deep is `O(n)` space even if you allocate nothing.

Interviewers often follow "can you do it in O(1) extra space?" That means: no new array or map, work in place with pointers.

## Hidden costs in library calls

| Call | Cost |
|---|---|
| `arr.push` / `append` | O(1) amortised |
| `arr.shift()` (JS) / `list.pop(0)` (Python) | O(n), everything shifts |
| `arr.includes(x)` / `x in list` | O(n) |
| `set.has(x)` / `x in set` | O(1) average |
| `str.slice` / `arr.slice` | O(k) copy |
| `string += char` in a loop | O(n²) total in many languages |
| `arr.sort()` | O(n log n) |

## Amortised analysis

A dynamic array doubles its capacity when full. A single `push` can cost `O(n)` (the copy), but copies happen rarely: total copy cost over n pushes is `1 + 2 + 4 + ... + n < 2n`. So each push is **O(1) amortised**. Amortised means *average over a sequence of operations*, with no randomness involved.

## Worked example

```js
function f(arr) {            // n = arr.length
  const sorted = [...arr].sort((a, b) => a - b); // O(n log n) time, O(n) space
  let count = 0;
  for (let i = 1; i < sorted.length; i++) {      // O(n)
    if (sorted[i] === sorted[i - 1]) count++;
  }
  return count;
}
```

Sequential blocks add: `O(n log n) + O(n) = O(n log n)`. Space is `O(n)` for the copy.

diagrams.title: Merge sort recursion tree: log n levels, n work per level

keyPoints: Add sequential blocks, multiply nested ones, then drop constants and smaller terms.
Two pointers with a while inside a for is still O(n): each pointer only moves forward.
Recursion cost = number of calls times work per call; draw the recursion tree.
Recursion depth costs stack space: n-deep recursion is O(n) space even with no arrays.
Watch hidden costs: shift, includes, slice and string concatenation in loops.

check.why: Two half-size subproblems plus a linear merge: log n levels of n work gives O(n log n).

check.q: A function recurses n levels deep and allocates nothing else. Its extra space is:
check.why: Each active call has a stack frame, so n nested calls use O(n) stack space.

check.q: Why is a dynamic array's push O(1) amortised even though resizing copies n items?
options: Doubling means total copy work over n pushes is under 2n
The copy happens in a background thread
check.why: Copies of size 1, 2, 4 ... n sum to less than 2n, so the average per push is constant.
